title: Dold–Kan simplicial realization of a dg category
statement:
Fix a commutative ring $\Lambda$ and universes as in [def-weil-size-convention]. For a cochain complex $E$ of $\Lambda$-modules [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], let $t(E)$ be the nonnegative chain complex with $t(E)_m=E^{-m}$ for $m>0$, $t(E)_0=\ker(d_E^0)$, and differential induced by $d_E$. Normalized chains give an equivalence from simplicial $\Lambda$-modules to nonnegative chain complexes; write $\Gamma$ for its inverse. The underlying simplicial set $S(E)=\Gamma t(E)$ is Kan, with natural identifications $\pi_0S(E)=H^0(E)$ and $\pi_m(S(E),0)=H^{-m}(E)$ for $m\ge1$. Translation identifies the groups at every vertex with those at zero. For a cochain map $E\to F$, $S(E)\to S(F)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence precisely when all maps $H^r(E)\to H^r(F)$ for $r\le0$ are isomorphisms; Kan complexes and weak equivalences use [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones].

Let $\mathcal B$ be any small dg $\Lambda$-category: its morphisms are cochain complexes, with associative unital chain-map composition and closed degree-zero identities. Applying $S$ to its morphism complexes gives a simplicial category $\mathcal B_\Delta$, with the same objects, composition induced by the Alexander–Whitney lax monoidal structure of $S$, and identity vertices the given identities. This construction is natural in dg functors. The coherent nerve $N_{\mathrm{hc}}(\mathcal B_\Delta)$, using the coherent-nerve construction of [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison], realizes the underlying infinity category of the dg category $\mathcal B$, compatibly with its closed degree-zero arrows and composition. The mapping comparisons are natural in dg functors and composition.

source.place: Stacks Tag 019G, theorem-dold-kan, for the normalization equivalence. Additional simplicial realization and homotopy clauses: Lurie, Higher Algebra (2017), Remark 1.2.3.14, Remark 1.3.1.12, Construction 1.3.1.13, Remark 1.3.1.14 and Proposition 1.3.1.17, printed pp. 82–85; Choudhury–Gallauer, Homotopy theory of dg sheaves, arXiv:1511.02828, Fact 3.14(3)–(4), printed p. 11. Read online 2026-10-17; archives WANTED in report.md. Tag 019G asserts only the equivalence, not the additional clauses.

proof.text: The corestriction of $d_E^{-1}$ to $\ker d_E^0$ exists since $d_E^0d_E^{-1}=0$; the other differentials are those of $E$, so $t(E)$ is a chain complex. Directly taking kernels modulo images gives $H_0(t(E))=\ker d_E^0/\operatorname{im}d_E^{-1}=H^0(E)$. For $m>1$ the adjacent three terms are unchanged, giving $H_m(t(E))=H^{-m}(E)$. For $m=1$, corestricting $d_E^{-1}$ to the kernel does not change its kernel; its incoming image is still $\operatorname{im}d_E^{-2}$, giving the same formula. A cochain map restricts to degree-zero kernels and commutes with these quotient identifications, so all of this is natural.

source.place: Section 3.3, the connective truncation adjunction following Fact 3.14, with chain degree m equal to cochain degree -m.

proof.text: Modules satisfy the stated abelian-category axioms: Hom sets are additive groups with bilinear composition, the zero module is a zero object, finite biproducts are direct sums, kernels are submodule kernels, and cokernels are quotients by images. A monomorphism is injective, since an element of its kernel gives a map from the free rank-one module that it kills; an epimorphism is surjective, since otherwise its nonzero quotient-by-image map would distinguish it from zero. Thus an injection identifies its source with the kernel of its quotient cokernel, and a surjection identifies its target with the cokernel of its kernel: the map from the quotient by its kernel to its image sends an element class to its image and is bijective. Apply the normalization equivalence to modules and put $S(E)=\Gamma t(E)$, forgetting the module structure only when taking the underlying simplicial set. Its counit gives $N(S(E))\cong t(E)$ naturally. We will also use its concrete simplex model. For any nonnegative chain complex $C$, full faithfulness and the counit identify $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}}(N(F(n)),C)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{sMod}}(F(n),\Gamma C)$. The latter is exactly $(\Gamma C)_n$: a simplicial linear map is determined by the image $x$ of the identity $[n]\to[n]$ and sends the basis vector $\theta:[r]\to[n]$ to $(\Gamma C)(\theta)x$; this formula gives the inverse. The natural chain isomorphism $q_n$ in the simplex input consequently identifies $(\Gamma C)_n$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ch}}(P(n),C)$. The simplicial operators are precomposition with $P(\alpha)$, and maps in $C$ are postcomposition. This fixes the inverse model and its comparisons naturally, without choosing values from an unproved existence assertion.

source.place: Lemma 1.2.3.12 and Lemma 1.2.3.13; normalized simplex representability derived here explicitly from the normalization equivalence.

proof.text: Here is the Kan argument, including outer horns. Write $X=S(E)$ and let $x_i\in X_{n-1}$, $i\ne k$, satisfy $d_i x_j=d_{j-1}x_i$ for $i<j$, the compatibility equations for a horn. Start with $u=0\in X_n$. Successively for $r=0,\ldots,k-1$ replace $u$ by $u+s_r(x_r-d_ru)$. The simplicial identities give $d_rs_r=\mathrm{id}$; for $i<r$, $d_i(x_r-d_ru)=d_{r-1}(x_i-d_iu)=0$, so earlier prescribed faces stay fixed. Next, for $r=n,n-1,\ldots,k+1$, replace $u$ by $u+s_{r-1}(x_r-d_ru)$. This fixes face $r$ since $d_rs_{r-1}=\mathrm{id}$, preserves faces $i<k$ by the same compatibility equations, and preserves faces $i>r$ because $d_{i-1}(x_r-d_ru)=d_r(x_i-d_iu)=0$. The final $u$ fills the horn. Empty loops cover $k=0,n$, including $n=1$. The face/degeneracy identities used are obtained by applying the simplicial functor to the corresponding equalities of monotone maps.

source.place: Stacks Tag 08NZ, lemma-simplicial-group-kan: its two horn-correction inductions written additively.

proof.text: Apply the Moore-cycle homotopy theorem to $X=S(E)$ and combine its natural identifications with $N\Gamma t(E)\cong t(E)$ and step 1. This gives the claimed components and positive homotopy groups, with no boundedness condition on $E$. For a vertex $a$, translation in degree $n$ by the constant degeneracy of $a$ is a simplicial isomorphism sending zero to $a$, with inverse translation by $-a$; it identifies all based groups. For a map $f:E\to F$, additivity gives $S(f)(x+a)=S(f)(x)+S(f)(a)$, so the identifications commute with the induced based maps. It follows that isomorphisms on $H^r$ for all $r\leq0$ give a bijection on components and isomorphisms on groups at every vertex, and the converse follows at zero. Every point of the realization lies in a realized simplex and is joined inside that simplex to a vertex. For completeness, a path from a vertex $v$ to a point $p$ changes the base point of a cube representative by rescaling that representative to an inner cube and mapping the surrounding radial collar along the path, from $v$ on its inner boundary to $p$ on its outer boundary. This construction respects relative-boundary homotopies; the reversed path gives its inverse because a path followed by its reverse contracts relative to its endpoints. Postcomposing the cube and its collar with the realized map is exactly the collar construction for the image path, so the induced homotopy-group maps are conjugate by these base-point isomorphisms. Thus the same criterion holds for all base points as required by the definition of weak homotopy equivalence.

source.place: Fact 3.14(3)–(4), plus the translation and base-point arguments written here; comparison is with realization homotopy groups, not merely algebraic chain homotopies.

proof.text: In the simplex model define the binary map on two simplices $a:P(n)\to t(E)$ and $b:P(n)\to t(F)$ by $(a\otimes b)D_n$, followed by $t(E)\otimes t(F)\to t(E\otimes F)$. The last chain map is induced by the degreewise maps of the nonpositive cochain terms into the full complexes, using the degree-zero cycle inclusions; in degree zero its image is a cycle since both factors are cycles. Explicitly, the tensor cochain complex has $(E\otimes F)^r=\bigoplus_{i+j=r}E^i\otimes_\Lambda F^j$ and $d(e\otimes f)=d_Ee\otimes f+(-1)^i e\otimes d_Ff$ for $e\in E^i$. The tensor of the truncations has the direct-sum terms and differential defined in the simplex input. Its sign $(-1)^p$ in chain degree $p$ equals $(-1)^{-p}$ in cochain degree $-p$, so the displayed maps commute with differentials, including the corestriction into cycles at degree zero. The chain-map assertion for $D_n$ makes the composite a chain map. Naturality of $D_n$ makes this binary operation simplicial and natural in $E,F$. The unit is $\epsilon_n:P(n)\to\Lambda[0]$. Coassociativity says both triple products use $(a\otimes b\otimes c)(D_n\otimes\mathrm{id})D_n=(a\otimes b\otimes c)(\mathrm{id}\otimes D_n)D_n$; the counit equations give the two unit equations. The degreewise maps respect the tensor associators and unit because each sends every pure tensor to the same pure tensor in the total complex. These formulas give precisely the Alexander–Whitney lax monoidal structure of $S$.

source.place: Construction 1.2.3.22 and Example 1.2.3.26; Construction 1.3.1.13. No symmetric monoidal assertion is used.

proof.text: For objects $x,y$ of $\mathcal B$, set $\mathcal B_\Delta(x,y)=S(\mathcal B(x,y))$. For $b:P(n)\to t\mathcal B(y,z)$ and $a:P(n)\to t\mathcal B(x,y)$ their composite is the chain map $m(b\otimes a)D_n$, where $m$ is the given dg composition, corestricted to the connective truncation. Its degree-zero value is a cycle by the chain-map property of dg composition. The two triple composites agree by the coassociativity equation in step 5 and the associativity of $m$. The identity at $x$ is the simplex $\mathrm{id}_x\epsilon_n$; the two counit equations and the dg unit equations verify both identity laws. At $n=0$ the formula is exactly the given composition of closed degree-zero arrows, since $P(0)=\Lambda[0]$ and $D_0[0]=[0]\otimes[0]$. A dg functor acts on these chain maps by postcomposition with its Hom-complex maps; these preserve $m$ and identities, so they define a simplicial functor. The equality of postcomposition and precomposition with each $P(\alpha)$ proves naturality for all simplex operators, and the same displayed formulas prove compatibility with composition.

source.place: Construction 1.3.1.13 and Remark 1.3.1.14; enriched associativity, units and dg-functor naturality verified using the explicit chain diagonal.

proof.text: All mapping simplicial sets of $\mathcal B_\Delta$ are Kan by step 3, and they and the object set are small in the fixed universes. Apply the locally Kan clause of the coherent-nerve comparison. It gives a quasicategory $N_{\mathrm{hc}}(\mathcal B_\Delta)$ and natural equivalences $S(\mathcal B(x,y))\simeq\operatorname{Map}_{N_{\mathrm{hc}}(\mathcal B_\Delta)}(x,y)$ sending vertices to their edges and respecting enriched composition with its coherent homotopies. This is the simplicial-realization presentation of the underlying infinity category of the dg category: its objects, mapping objects and composition are obtained from the dg enrichment by the construction in steps 2 and 5–6, followed by the coherent-nerve presentation theorem. In particular its homotopy category has morphisms $H^0\mathcal B(x,y)$ by step 4, and its actual mapping spaces retain all $H^{-m}$, rather than only these components. Naturality for simplicial functors in the cited comparison, applied to the dg-functor construction in step 6, gives the asserted naturality and coherent compatibility with composition.

source.place: Construction 1.3.1.13 and Remark 1.3.1.14, with the locally Kan coherent-nerve presentation and mapping comparison supplied by lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison. The underlying infinity category is expressed in its simplicial-realization model.
